Your original post was in opposition to the very idea of a minimum wage.

Suppose, right now, we abolished it. Your treatment of labor as a commodity, subject to supply and demand, suggests that--because we have a labor glut--wages would fall. You argue that wages have no price floor. So, as long as someone is willing to work for less, they will be paid less.

Your position is one you could only take if you think wages should fall. So, you expect they would. This necessarily decreases the spending power of workers in the economy.

Suppose you have 9 workers, and the minimum wage is abolished. You lower their wages, and some leave. You hire others, and now for the same cost:output ratio, you have 12 workers. Those workers are making less than the 9 you had before. They each have less money to spend than the 9 you used to employ. Unless you are agreeing that prices levels across the economy would drop (the VERY DEFINITION of deflation), then each of your 12 workers has less spending power in the economy than the 9 had before. But, each of the 12 has roughly the same cost of living as your 9 did when you had 9. Either prices fall, or their non-necessary spending decreases.

Now, suppose every business did this. In order to sell what you are producing, you have to lower your prices.
